findings.title: How exposure management can help public sector prepare for PHP2Shell-like vulnerabilities
findings.summary: PHP2Shell showed how fast a runtime-level flaw can go from disclosure to confirmed exploitation. Here’s how federal, state, local, and education teams can prepare for PHP2Shell-like flaws. Key takeaways PHP2Shell went from disclosure to confirmed exploitation within days. With AI shortening the disclosure-to-exploitation window, new critical flaws will likely move just as fast. Most security teams’ primary challenge with PHP2Shell was knowing where the vulnerabilities were in their environment. Teams that already knew where PHP ran across their IT infrastructure, web applications, and cloud assets were in a position to act quickly. Initial access flaws will continue to impact your network edge, so work backward from the foothold. Map what an attacker could reach after breaching an edge device, such as root access, management servers, and directory services. Then close those escalation paths by patching kernels and restricting unprivileged user namespaces. To prioritize, factor in exploitation evidence, not severity alone. Weigh KEV status, exploit prediction scores, and your own internet exposure, as well as pre-approve a plan for systems you can’t patch immediately. When two critical PHP vulnerabilities, nicknamed PHP2Shell , leaked ahead of their coordinated disclosure date on Oct. 20, and their alarming scope and severity became clear, cybersecurity teams sprung into “all hands on deck” mode, much in the same way they did in late 2021 in response to the Log4Shell bug. Many organizations, including government agencies, rushed to take down their websites as an early, stopgap preventive measure against attackers’ already active attempts to exploit these two memory management vulnerabilities, which were cataloged as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and given a CVSS score of 9.2. Thrust into a furious race against time, security teams scrambled to detect and patch their instances of PHP, the popular server-side scripting language that around 70% of websites use . I

findings.title: Metasploit Wrap Up: Breaking Zimbra's Identity Boundaries
findings.summary: This release we have three pull requests from jburgess-r7 building out coverage for the identity-boundary issues detailed in Rapid7's Breaking Zimbra Identity Boundaries, Part One research. First up is a new shared mixin, Msf::Exploit::Remote::HTTP::Zimbra , which gives every current and future Zimbra module a common foundation for account/admin SOAP authentication, canonical identity resolution, mailbox-server lookup, and version parsing, allowing future modules to stay focused on the vulnerability instead of re-implementing Zimbra's SOAP plumbing. Built on top of that mixin are two new modules targeting CVEs from the same research track: CVE-2026-73571 ( #22080 ) It's an authorization bypass in Zimbra's SaveDraftRequest handling that lets an ordinary authenticated user send mail as another local mailbox without a delegation grant, landing a message in the victim's own Sent folder in the process. CVE-2026-93637 ( #22070 ) Is a rate-limit bypass in Zimbra's Network Edition GraphQL authentication endpoint, which lets credential-stuffing attempts skip the source-IP lockout counter that normally protects the SOAP login path. Both modules were validated against live Zimbra 10.1.16 Network Edition instances. Super cool contributions from our very own jburgess-r7 . findings.title: netty-incubator-codec-ohttp: OHTTP codecs retain consumed outer cumulation buffers after completed exchanges
findings.summary:
## Summary:

OHttpClientCodec and OHttpServerCodec retain the encrypted outer HttpContent in a handler-level cumulationBuffer. After a valid OHTTP exchange completes, the OHTTP request/response context is destroyed, but the outer cumulationBuffer is not released or reset. It remains referenced by the codec until a later inbound content frame replaces it or the handler is removed/channel is closed.

This can pin attacker-influenced pooled/direct buffer capacity on idle keep-alive channels. Across many long-lived idle connections, this can create availability pressure.

Affected components:

* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpClientCodec.java
* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpServerCodec.java
* codec-ohttp/src/main/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpRequestResponseContext.java

## Root cause:

OHttpClientCodec retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer. On LastHttpContent, it destroys only the OHttpRequestResponseContextHolder. The cumulationBuffer is released in handlerRemoved(), not immediately after successful exchange completion.

OHttpServerCodec follows the same pattern: it retains inbound content into a handler-level cumulationBuffer, and on completed request/response it destroys the OHttpRequestResponseContext. The outer cumulationBuffer remains owned by the codec and is released only when the handler is removed.

OHttpRequestResponseContext.parse() consumes bytes from the caller-provided outer cumulation buffer, but its destroy() path releases only the inner binary HTTP cumulation, not the codec-level outer cumulationBuffer.

## PoC:

A local test only:

```
codec-ohttp/src/test/java/io/netty/incubator/codec/ohttp/OHttpCumulationBufferRetentionTest.java
```

The test reuses existing OHTTP test helpers and BouncyCastle crypto provider to perform valid completed OHTTP exchanges over EmbeddedChannel pairs. It sends both a small and a large request/response exchange, confirms comp

findings.title: storyblok-backup: Stored path traversal via unsanitized Storyblok component names in backup output
findings.summary:
### Summary
storyblok-backup writes files using unsanitized names for Storyblok components, which are content type or schema definitions. This allows a component name containing path traversal sequences to cause backup files to be written outside the intended backup directory. Anyone with component management access in the source Storyblok space, not server access, can plant a malicious component name that causes arbitrary file writes on the machine of anyone who later runs a backup against that space.

### Details
The writeJson function, which takes a folder, a file name, and content, builds the output file path by directly concatenating the backup directory, the folder, and the file name as strings, with no path sanitization or containment check.

For the components resource type specifically, the file name used is the component's own name field, which is free text and editable by anyone with component management access in the Storyblok CMS.

Other resource types are not affected by this same issue. Stories and datasources use their numeric IDs as filenames, and assets have their filename derived by splitting on the slash character and taking the last segment, which strips path separators. This issue is scoped specifically to components.

Since the component name is stored in Storyblok and only read back later when the backup tool runs, this is a stored, second order vulnerability. The malicious value is planted once, then triggers on every subsequent backup run performed by anyone using this tool against that Storyblok space.

### PoC

**Step 1 — plant the malicious component name via Storyblok's Management API:**

curl -X POST "https://mapi.storyblok.com/v1/spaces/<SPACE_ID>/components/" \
  -H "Authorization: <MANAGEMENT_API_TOKEN>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "component": {
      "name": "../../../../tmp/evil-storyblok-backup",
      "schema": {}
    }
  }'

findings.title: TeamPass folder re-parenting authorization bypass
findings.summary:
## Summary

Missing authorization in the update_folder action: any authenticated non-read-only user can rename, re-parent and convert to personal any folder in the instance, moving another team's credential subtree into their own personal space and removing it from the organization. Confirmed at HEAD 2f271cdd (3.2.1.1), and present at 3.1.3.1 and 3.1.7.6.

## The defect

The folder-management endpoint dispatches an update_folder action that renames and re-parents a folder. Unlike its sibling actions in the same file, it never checks the edited folder id or the submitted parent id against the caller's accessible-folder set, and the file itself performs no session/authorization gate at all. By pointing the new parent at their own personal folder, an authenticated low-privilege user takes ownership of any folder in the instance.

app/sources/folders.queries.php:
- The file never calls the session/authorization helpers: a grep for checkSession and userAccessPage across the whole file returns zero hits.
- case 'update_folder' (lines 294-662) contains no reference to the caller's user-accessible_folders set. The only access-related logic is the personal-folder computation at lines 428-468 and the guard at line 503, which short-circuits on `(int) $isPersonal === 1`.
- The sibling actions do carry the check: case 'add_folder' validates against user-accessible_folders at line 743, case 'delete_folders' at line 904, and case 'copy_folder' applies the equivalent parent check.

So update_folder is the one folder-mutating action in the file without an authorization predicate on either the target folder id or the new parent id.

## Attacker model and trace

An authenticated TeamPass user who is not read-only (no administrative role required). The attacker submits update_folder with the victim folder's id and a parentId pointing at their own personal folder. Because the new parent is personal, the personal-folder computation sets $isPersonal = 1, which satisfies the line 503 guard

findings.title: Refitter: Unrestricted OpenAPI references permit build-host SSRF and file inclusion
findings.summary:
### Summary

Refitter (the `refitter` dotnet tool, built on NJsonSchema for `$ref` resolution) fetches remote
`http(s)` URLs and reads local files (including absolute paths and `../` traversal outside the input
directory), inlining the referenced schema into the generated Refit interface/contracts. Running
`refitter <spec> --output Out.cs` on a spec whose `$ref` points at an attacker/internal URL or an
arbitrary local file yields SSRF, remote file inclusion, and local file inclusion. Verified on
Refitter 2.0.0.

### Details

- `$ref: http://attacker-or-internal/evil.json#/...` -> build host fetches (SSRF) and inlines the
  remote schema (RFI); confirmed property `REMOTE_REFIT_PROP`.
- `$ref: /abs/path.json#/...` or `../../secret.json#/...` -> out-of-tree local file read + inlined
  (LFI); confirmed property `REFIT_LFI_MARKER`. Both absolute and relative traversal work.

No RCE: Refitter emits Refit interfaces with no baseUrl string literal (Refit sets the base address at
runtime), enum values use C# verbatim-string doubling, and string defaults are escaped. The chain
stops at SSRF + RFI + LFI.

The `$ref` resolution is performed by Refitter's NJsonSchema dependency, which Refitter ships and
invokes with these unsafe defaults.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`, `listener.py`) attached: installs the .NET SDK + Refitter if needed,
confirms LFI (out-of-tree read), SSRF (listener hit during generation), and RFI (remote schema
inlined). Verified on 2.0.0.

### Impact

Build-time SSRF (CWE-918) from the developer or CI host, disclosure of arbitrary local files
(CWE-22), and inclusion of untrusted remote content (CWE-829), from running Refitter on an
attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description. No code execution. Estimated
Medium-High, e.g. `[reproduce.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29395269/reproduce.sh)` (the CNA sets the final score).

### Suggested fix

Don't resolve remote `$ref`s by default (opt-in + host allowlist); confine

ALTCHA: Nil-map panic (pre-verification DoS) in v1 parseServerSignature on malformed VerificationData
findings.summary:
### Summary

`parseServerSignature` in the v1 module only initializes `ServerSignatureVerificationData.Extra` inside the `if err == nil` branch after `url.ParseQuery(parsedPayload.VerificationData)`. Go's `url.ParseQuery` returns the successfully-parsed pairs together with a non-nil error when the query string contains a malformed percent-escape. A subsequent loop unconditionally writes unknown keys into `Extra`, regardless of `err`, causing a nil-map write panic (assignment to entry in nil map) whenever an attacker supplies a `VerificationData` string with a bad %-escape (e.g. `x=1&%zz=2`).

This is reachable pre-authentication: `parseServerSignature` is called by the exported `VerifyServerSignature` / `VerifyServerSignatureSafe` before any HMAC/signature check, and `VerificationData` is attacker-controlled data forwarded by the client as part of the ALTCHA server-signature payload.

### Impact

Any application calling `VerifyServerSignature` or `VerifyServerSignatureSafe` on unauthenticated input can be made to panic by submitting a crafted payload. Under standard net/http, the per-request goroutine panic is recovered and the request aborts (a log-flood / per-request DoS); it escalates to a full process crash if verification runs in an application-spawned goroutine or a non-recovering framework.

### Proof Of Concept

```go
payload, _ := json.Marshal(ServerSignaturePayload{
    Algorithm:        SHA256,
    VerificationData: "x=1&%zz=2",
    Signature:        "irrelevant",
    Verified:         true,
})
encoded := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(payload)
VerifyServerSignature(encoded, "some-secret") // panics: assignment to entry in nil map

```

### Patch

`Extra` is now initialized unconditionally before the `url.ParseQuery` error check, so it's always safe to write into regardless of parse errors.

### Workarounds

Recover from panics around calls to `VerifyServerSignature`/`VerifyServerSignatureSafe`, or reject/sanitize `VerificationData` before calling them

findings.title: falcon-rust: Discrete-Gaussian sampler runs at 2^-33 precision, far below Falcon's requirement (reference KAT vectors no longer pass)
findings.summary:
**Reporter:** Connor Webber
**Package:** `falcon-rust` (crates.io), repository `github.com/aszepieniec/falcon-rust`
**Affected:** v0.1.3 and the current `master` (HEAD `cfa1b35`). Regression introduced in commit `bf2cf00`.
**Component:** discrete-Gaussian sampler, `src/samplerz.rs` (`approx_exp`, `ber_exp`, `sampler_z`)
**Status:** Confirmed by source review and by empirical measurement of the crate's own compiled code.

## Summary

falcon-rust's discrete-Gaussian rejection sampler evaluates its `exp()` acceptance step at only 32 bits of fractional precision. Measured directly against the crate's own compiled code, `approx_exp` has a maximum relative error of 2^-33. For comparison, the Falcon reference implementation achieves about 2^-63, and the f64 code this crate replaced achieved about 2^-52. The current sampler is therefore roughly 2^19 (about 500,000x) less precise than the version it replaced, and about 2^30 less precise than the reference.

Falcon's security proof relies on the sampled signatures being statistically indistinguishable from an ideal discrete Gaussian, so the signature transcript leaks nothing about the secret trapdoor. That guarantee holds only when the sampler's relative error stays small enough, over the roughly 2^64 signature budget, to keep the Renyi divergence between the real and ideal distributions negligible. The precision the security analysis relies on is cited in the literature between roughly 2^-40 and 2^-46 (for example the FACCT and isochronous-sampling analyses). At 2^-33 the sampler is below every value in that range, roughly 128x to 4096x too coarse depending on which bound you take, so the precondition the proof depends on is not met.

There is a second, bound-independent piece of evidence that removes any ambiguity: the crate's sampler can no longer reproduce Falcon's known-answer test (KAT) vectors, which are the authoritative correctness oracle. Rather than restore the precision, the maintainers loosened their own test tol

findings.title: Bolt: Prevent SSRF due to unchecked followed redirects
findings.summary:
### Impact

The `/bolt/async/upload-url` and `/bolt/async/embed` endpoints validated only the **submitted** URL before fetching it server-side, but the fetch then **followed redirects to destinations that were never re-validated**. This allowed an authenticated user to bypass the SSRF guard (`UrlSafetyChecker`) and make the server issue requests to internal/cloud-metadata addresses.

### Patches

This issue has been patched with Bolt 6.1.5.

findings.summary:
Standalone `streamable-http` mode in `datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server` rejects forged `Host` and `Origin` headers on `/mcp`, but custom management routes mounted on the same application do not get the same browser-origin protection. A malicious website can keep an attacker origin while its hostname resolves to `127.0.0.1` or a private target address, then send `PUT /api/connect` to replace the MCP server's active Jupyter backend. The route accepts the browser-shaped request and makes the server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure.

The protected `/mcp` endpoint shows the intended browser-origin boundary. With `MCP_TOKEN` configured, `/mcp` rejects forged browser headers:

```text
POST /mcp with Authorization: Bearer SCAN_MCP_TOKEN
Host: attacker.example:8142
Origin: http://attacker.example:8142

HTTP 421 Invalid Host header
```

The vulnerable route is `jupyter_mcp_server/server.py:143-187`. It parses caller JSON, updates the active Jupyter backend configuration, resets `ServerContext`, and starts the kernel without applying the `/mcp` Host/Origin rejection to the custom route:

```python
    document_runtime = DocumentRuntime(**data)

        provider=document_runtime.provider,
        runtime_url=document_runtime.runtime_url,
        runtime_id=document_runtime.runtime_id,
        runtime_token=document_runtime.runtime_token,
        document_url=document_runtime.document_url,
        document_id=document_runtime.document_id,
        document_token=document_runtime.document_token,
        allowed_jupyter_tools=document_runtime.allowed_jupyter_tools or "notebook_run-all-cells,notebook_get-selected-cell"
    )

    ServerContext.reset()

    try:
        __start_kernel()
        return JSONResponse({"success": True})
```

findings.summary:
Standalone `streamable-http` mode in `datalayer/jupyter-mcp-server` requires `MCP_TOKEN` for `/mcp`, but the custom management routes mounted on the same application do not enforce that token. An unauthenticated network caller can invoke `PUT /api/connect`, choose the Jupyter backend URL and token fields, reset the server context, and make the MCP server start a kernel client against attacker-controlled infrastructure. The same missing authentication affects the state-changing `DELETE /api/stop` route.

The intended authentication boundary is documented in the security guide and enforced during startup:

findings.title: Flyto2 Core: SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding (validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning)
findings.summary:
# [MEDIUM] SSRF guard bypass via DNS rebinding — validate_url_ssrf resolves-then-connects without pinning

- **CWE:** CWE-918 (SSRF) / CWE-367 (TOCTOU).
- **CVSS v3.1:** `AV:N/AC:H/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:L/A:N` = **6.8 Medium** (AC:H — needs attacker-controlled DNS with a low/zero TTL and to flip the answer between the guard's lookup and the connection's lookup; S:C — reaches internal/metadata services the guard is meant to block; C:H — e.g. cloud metadata credentials at 169.254.169.254).

## Summary
`http.paginate` validates only the initial `base_url`, then follows server-supplied pagination targets (RFC 5988 `Link: rel="next"` headers, cursor/offset URLs) in a loop **without revalidating each follow-up URL**. An attacker's first-page response can point `next` at an internal address, causing a second-order SSRF whose internal body is aggregated into the returned items.

## Root Cause
`src/core/modules/atomic/http/paginate.py:495` validates `base_url` (first URL only). The pagination loop `_paginate_link_header` reads `next_url` via `_parse_link_header` (:203), sets `url=next_url` (:208), and calls `session.request(method, url)` (:196) with NO validate call in the loop (:186-208 has zero guard calls).

## Impact
Readable second-order SSRF that bypasses the SSRF control; internal/metadata body aggregated into `all_items` and returned to the caller (C:H, S:C).

Verified live: `http.paginate` with allowlisted base `127.0.0.1` followed a `Link: <http://127.0.0.3/...>; rel="next"` (non-allowlisted) and returned `INTERNAL-NEXTPAGE-SECRET` in the aggregated items.

findings.summary:
## Summary
`validate_url_ssrf` resolves the hostname, checks the IP against private ranges, then **discards the IP and returns the hostname URL string**. aiohttp performs a fresh, independent DNS resolution at connect time. An attacker controlling DNS for a hostname (TTL 0, alternating public IP and internal IP) passes validation on the first lookup and connects to the internal IP on the second — a classic check-then-use race. SECURITY_SSRF.md line 63 explicitly claims DNS-rebinding is prevented; it is not.

## Root Cause
`src/core/utils.py:523` returns the hostname URL after validation; the resolved IP is never pinned. A repo grep of `http/` and `utils.py` for `TCPConnector` / `resolver` / `response.history` / `on_request_redirect` / IP-pinning returns NONE. Each module builds a fresh `ClientSession` per call → the connect-time `getaddrinfo` is independent of the validation-time lookup.

Defeats the SSRF guard on ALL modules that call it (readable internal fetch). Independent of IP-range completeness — the private IP is never presented to `is_private_ip`. Requires attacker DNS control + winning the resolution race → AC:H.

Code-proven: `validate_url_ssrf` returns the hostname (utils.py:523); no pinned-IP connector anywhere. Two independent resolutions occur (validation-time and aiohttp connect-time).

findings.title: django-docutils unsafe Docutils defaults allow local file disclosure, SSRF, and stored XSS
findings.summary:
## Summary

django-docutils before `0.30.0` rendered reStructuredText through Docutils without protected web-safe defaults. Public rendering paths, including `publish_doctree`, `publish_html_from_source`, `publish_html_from_doctree`, `publish_parts_from_doctree`, the `{% rst %}` template tag, the `rst` template filter, `DocutilsTemplates`, and `DocutilsView`, could process attacker-controlled RST with Docutils directives that read local files, fetch URL-backed content, or emit raw HTML.

The issue is fixed in `0.30.0` by disabling Docutils file insertion, raw directives, local `docutils.conf` processing, and unsafe URI schemes by default, and by sanitizing doctrees before HTML is emitted.

Applications are affected when they render attacker-controlled or lower-trust RST through django-docutils without their own safe Docutils configuration. Applications that only render trusted static RST are not affected unless that content can be influenced by an attacker.

## Impact

An attacker who can influence RST rendered by a vulnerable django-docutils integration may be able to read files readable by the Django worker process, trigger server-side requests through URL-backed directives, or inject raw HTML/JavaScript into rendered output.

Examples of affected application patterns include comments, wiki pages, blog bodies, profile or biography fields, CMS fields, uploaded RST documents, API-supplied RST, or overridden view content methods that return user-supplied RST.

Potential impact includes disclosure of application configuration, environment files, credentials, source files, templates, mounted secrets, and logs readable by the process. UI escaping after rendering is not sufficient for file disclosure because the server-side read occurs before HTML reaches the client.

## Affected versions

Affected package: `django-docutils` on PyPI

Affected versions: `<= 0.29.0`

Patched versions: `>= 0.30.0`

Before `0.30.0`, django-docutils handed RST content to

findings.title: Jane: $ref resolution performs SSRF + LFI (path traversal) at code-generation time (jane-php)
findings.summary:
### Summary
jane-php resolves external `$ref` targets at code-generation time via `file_get_contents($ref)` (jane-php/json-schema-runtime/Reference.php::doResolve) with no scheme/path restriction. An attacker-controlled OpenAPI document can therefore cause: `$ref: 'http://attacker/x'` -> SSRF (HTTP GET at gen time; response inlined = RFI); `$ref: '/abs/file'` -> LFI; `$ref: '../secret.yaml'` -> path-traversal LFI (CWE-22, arbitrary local JSON/YAML read). Verified 7.11.2/PHP8.1 (listener records the fetch; remote + `../` local content inlined into the generated code). `file://` rejected. CWE-918/CWE-98/CWE-611/CWE-22.

### Details
```php
// Reference.php::doResolve()
$contents = file_get_contents($fragment); // $fragment = attacker-controlled $ref URI
```

### Impact
Generating PHP with jane from an attacker-influenced OpenAPI document issues HTTP requests to attacker-chosen URLs (SSRF — internal services, cloud metadata) and reads arbitrary local files (LFI via `../`), at build/CI time, inlining results into the output.

### PoC
`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`, `gen.php`): runs jane on a remote-$ref spec (local listener records the SSRF, output checked for the inlined response) and a `../`-traversal local-$ref spec (output checked for the leaked file).

### Suggested fix
Disable remote `$ref` fetching by default (or allow-list); confine local `$ref` to the spec directory (reject absolute paths and `..`). Don't `file_get_contents($ref)` on attacker-controlled URIs.

findings.title: Refitter allows arbitrary code execution through unescaped OpenAPI content-type values
findings.summary:
### Summary

Refitter emits the spec's content-type key (content map key in requestBody/responses) verbatim into a Refit `[Headers("Accept: <ct>", "Content-Type: <ct>")]` attribute string without escaping
`"`. A crafted value survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation, breaks out of the attribute and
the enclosing interface + namespace, injects a top-level `file class` with a `[ModuleInitializer]`
method, and reopens so the file stays valid. .NET runs `[ModuleInitializer]` methods at assembly
load, so the attacker's code executes at application startup. Verified on Refitter 2.0.0 / .NET 8.

The malicious input is a content-type KEY such as: content: { 'application/<breakout>': {schema} }.
No `--skip-validation` is required.

### PoC

`reproduce.sh` (+ `make_spec.py`) attached: generates with default validation, compiles into a
console app, runs it (Main does not touch the client), and shows a marker written at assembly load.

### Impact

Code execution at assembly load (process startup) in any application that compiles a Refitter client
generated from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description. Estimated Critical, e.g.
`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N` (the CNA sets the final score).

### Suggested fix

Escape every spec-derived string before emitting it into a Refit attribute (escape `"`, `\`,
reject newlines) and validate characters. We recommend auditing all attribute emissions that embed
spec-derived values, using one shared encoder.

findings.title: Refitter allows arbitrary code execution through unescaped OpenAPI paths
findings.summary:
### Summary

Refitter emits each OpenAPI path (the paths-object key) verbatim into a Refit `[Get("<path>")]`
attribute string, without escaping `"` or restricting characters. A crafted single-line, /-prefixed
path survives Refitter's default OpenAPI validation yet closes the attribute string and the enclosing
interface + namespace, injects a top-level `file class` with a `[ModuleInitializer]` method, and
reopens a namespace + interface so the file stays valid. .NET runs `[ModuleInitializer]` methods when
the generated assembly is loaded, so the attacker's code executes at application startup. Verified on
Refitter 2.0.0 / .NET 8.

### Details

```
[Get("/p")] Task<string> Dummy(); } }
file class Evil { [System.Runtime.CompilerServices.ModuleInitializer]
  internal static void Init(){ /* attacker code */ } }
namespace N2 { public partial interface I2 { [Get("/q")]
        Task<string> GetU(string id);
    }
}
```

No `--skip-validation` is needed (the payload is a valid single-line path). The generated `.cs` is
compiled into the victim application; the module initializer runs at assembly load. This is distinct
from the value sinks (enum/default), which are escaped; the path sink has no escaping. The
`[Header("<name>")]` attribute is likewise emitted raw (header parameter names), at minimum a
build-breaking DoS.

app, runs it (Main does not touch the client), and shows a marker written at assembly load. Verified

Code execution at assembly load (process startup) in any application that compiles a Refitter client
generated from an attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced OpenAPI description.

Escape the route template before emitting it into `[Get("…")]` (escape `"`, `\`, reject newlines) and
validate that paths contain only legal URI-template characters. Apply the same encoding to

findings.title: NATS Server allows unauthenticated memory exhaustion through incomplete MQTT CONNECT packets
findings.summary:
### Background

NATS.io is a high performance open source pub-sub distributed communication technology, built for the cloud, on-premise, IoT and edge computing.

The NATS Server supports MQTT clients, including authentication and parsing of MQTT `CONNECT` packets.

### Problem Description

An unauthenticated MQTT client could cause the server to retain large incomplete MQTT `CONNECT` packets before authentication completed.

The parser retained partial pre-authentication packet data while waiting for the advertised MQTT packet length to be completed. An attacker could therefore consume server memory until authentication timeouts closed the connections.

### Affected Versions

Versions v2.14.2, v2.12.11 and below are vulnerable. The issue is fixed in v2.14.3 and v2.12.12.

### Workarounds

Deployments not using MQTT are not affected. Deployments that need MQTT should upgrade to a fixed release.

### References

 * GHSA advisory: <https://github.com/nats-io/nats-server/security/advisories/GHSA-r72h-j7qq-v6qg>
 * Credit: Asritha Bodepudi, Trail of Bits

findings.title: snark-verifier: Halo 2 aggregation circuit mishandles point-at-infinity proof elements
findings.summary:
### Summary
The Halo 2 aggregation circuit could mishandle proof elements encoded as the point at infinity.

When an assigned proof point appeared in an MSM term with constant scalar one, the Halo 2 loader used a scalar-one shortcut that passed the assigned point directly into the EC sum helper. The EC sum implementation used by that path assumed its inputs were non-identity points, while assigned proof points could represent the encoded identity `(0, 0)`.

### Details
`EcPointLoader::multi_scalar_multiplication` partitions MSM terms by scalar and base type. For `(Value::Constant(ONE), Value::Assigned(_))`, the loader placed the assigned base into the non-scaled variable-base list and later passed those points to `sum_with_const`.

The default Halo 2 shim delegates `sum_with_const` to halo2-lib `EccChip::sum`. In affected versions, that sum helper used incomplete affine addition and assumed that every input point was non-identity. A prover-controlled proof point encoded as `(0, 0)` could therefore enter the final aggregation sum through the scalar-one shortcut and affect the MSM or accumulator computation.

The issue was fixed in halo2-lib by updating `EccChip::sum` to treat encoded identity inputs as no-ops and to return `(0, 0)` when the total sum is the identity. This removes the non-identity input precondition from callers such as the Halo 2 aggregation loader.

### Impact
Recursive aggregation circuits using the Halo 2 loader could compute an MSM or accumulator with an identity proof element in a path whose implementation assumed non-identity inputs. This breaks the expected handling of point-at-infinity proof elements in aggregation.

Practical exploitability depends on the surrounding aggregation and final-decider checks, so this is rated medium severity.

findings.title: NLTK: ARFF_Formatter Injects Weka ARFF Schema Directives via Attacker-Controlled Class Labels

### Summary

`nltk.classify.weka.ARFF_Formatter` writes class labels directly into the Weka ARFF `@ATTRIBUTE '-label-' {...}` declaration without any ARFF quoting or escaping. An attacker who can contribute class labels to a training dataset can include ARFF metacharacters such as `}`, newlines, `@ATTRIBUTE`, and `@DATA` to break out of the nominal label list and inject attacker‑controlled ARFF schema and data directives.

This vulnerability is reachable in any application that calls `WekaClassifier.train()` or `ARFF_Formatter.from_train()` with attacker‑influenced training data. The victim does not need to manually edit the ARFF file; the normal training workflow writes the malformed ARFF automatically.

The vulnerable code path is:

1. `WekaClassifier.train()` calls `ARFF_Formatter.from_train(featuresets)`.
2. `from_train()` extracts labels from the training data and passes them to `ARFF_Formatter(labels, features)`.
3. `header_section()` uses `",".join(self._labels)` directly, embedding attacker‑controlled strings into the ARFF header without sanitization.

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in DependencyGraph traversal causes denial of service via deep dependency chains
findings.summary:
## Root Cause
The dependency-graph traversal helpers recurse over dependency links without any depth
bound or visited set. `DependencyGraph._tree` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:404`)
recurses once per dependency link, `triples` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:432`) is a
recursive generator, and `get_cycle_path` (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:520`) recurses
over dependencies. The neighbouring `contains_cycle` method was deliberately rewritten as
an iterative depth-first search, but these sibling helpers on the public traversal path
were left recursive with no depth counter.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted CoNLL/Malt-TAB dependency structure and then walks
it via `tree()` or `triples()` aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`, terminating the
affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is pure
Python, so the result is a catchable `RecursionError`, not memory corruption or code
execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. `get_cycle_path` additionally
lacks a visited set and will not terminate on a genuine cycle.

## Attack Chain
1. The application constructs `DependencyGraph(conll_str)` from attacker-supplied text
   where token *k*'s head is token *k+1*, forming a linear dependency chain of length *N*.
   Graph construction (`_parse`) is iterative and completes without error.
2. The application calls the public `DependencyGraph.tree()`
   (`nltk/parse/dependencygraph.py:408`), which invokes `_tree(root)`.
3. `_tree` recurses once per chain link with no depth guard and no visited set, consuming
   one stack frame per link (the list comprehension costs roughly two frames per level).
4. Once the chain length exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled
   `RecursionError` propagates out of the public API. `triples()` fails the same way.

## Bypass Evidence
Against the shipped source at the default recursion limit, a chain of length 5 walks
cleanly through `tree()`, while a chain of length

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in semantic-logic type parser causes denial of service via nested type strings
findings.summary:
## Root Cause
The semantic-logic type parser `read_type` (`nltk/sem/logic.py:866`) recurses on both
halves of every `<a,b>` complex type (`nltk/sem/logic.py:882-884`) with no depth or length
bound — only an `isinstance` assertion and a parenthesis-balance assertion. The
`LogicParser.MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` guard (`nltk/sem/logic.py:107,294`) protects the expression
parser but never runs on the `read_type` path, which is reached directly by the public
`Type.fromstring` classmethod and by signature-string type checking.

## Impact
An application that parses an untrusted type string, or type-checks an expression against
an attacker-influenced signature, aborts with an unhandled `RecursionError`, terminating
the affected operation or request worker (denial of service, CWE-674). The recursion is
pure Python, yielding a catchable `RecursionError` rather than memory corruption or code
execution. Confidentiality and integrity are unaffected. Exposure is narrower than a
general-purpose parser because the input must reach a type-string or signature parameter.

## Attack Chain
1. The application calls `nltk.sem.logic.Type.fromstring(s)` (`nltk/sem/logic.py:736`) — or
   `Expression.typecheck(signature)` / `Expression.fromstring(expr, type_check=True,
   signature=...)`, which reach `read_type` for each type-string signature value
   (`nltk/sem/logic.py:1080`) — with a deeply nested type string such as
   `"<" * n + "e,e" + ">" * n`.
2. `Type.fromstring` passes the string straight to `read_type` with no length or depth
   check (only assertions on type and parenthesis balance).
3. `read_type` recurses on both halves of each `<a,b>` level, consuming one stack frame per
   nesting level; the `MAX_PARSE_DEPTH` guard on the separate `LogicParser` class does not
   execute here.
4. Once the depth exceeds the interpreter recursion limit, an unhandled `RecursionError`
   propagates out of the public API.

## Bypass Evidence
Running the shipped `read_type`/`ComplexType`/`Type` source verbatim

## Root Cause
`Tree.fromlist` (`nltk/tree/tree.py:767`) converts a nested list into a `Tree` by recursing
once per nesting level (`nltk/tree/tree.py:780`) with no depth bound — its only validation

builds `Tree` objects identically.

An application that builds a `Tree` from an attacker-controlled nested list — for example

The Toolbox settings-tree helpers recurse over the parsed element tree without any depth

findings.title: NLTK: Uncontrolled recursion in WordNet Synset hypernym walkers (max_depth/min_depth/hypernym_paths/hypernym_distances) causes DoS
findings.summary:
## Summary

Four hypernym-walking methods on the WordNet `Synset` class in `nltk/corpus/reader/wordnet.py` (`max_depth`, `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances`) traverse the hypernym pointer graph by direct recursion with no visited-node set and no depth cap. WordNet `data.<pos>` file content is untrusted corpus input in NLTK, the same trust boundary the project already treats as attacker-controlled across its corpus-content hardening work. When the parsed hypernym graph contains a cycle, or a chain deeper than the interpreter recursion limit, these methods recurse without bound and raise an uncaught `RecursionError`, aborting the traversal and any worker that does not catch it. No special privileges are needed; the victim only has to load an attacker-supplied corpus and call any of several shipped public methods that reach these walkers.

## Root Cause

`Synset.max_depth` computes `1 + max(h.max_depth() for h in hypernyms)` and only assigns its `_max_depth` memo after that recursive expression fully returns. Because Python evaluates the right-hand side completely before binding the left-hand side, the memo is never set on a node that is still on the recursion stack, so a cyclic graph re-enters the same not-yet-memoized node indefinitely. `min_depth`, `hypernym_paths`, and `hypernym_distances` follow the same recursive descent with no cycle detection. The security invariant that graph traversal over untrusted corpus data must terminate is violated: the pointer offsets parsed from the data file are stored verbatim with no graph-shape validation, so the attacker controls the graph topology. The sibling walkers in the same class (`closure`, `tree`, `_shortest_hypernym_paths`) were hardened with acyclic/visited guards, which shows cyclic hypernym graphs are an in-scope threat that these four methods simply were not converted to handle.

findings.title: NLTK: StreamBackedCorpusView constructor os.stat leaks out-of-root file existence, size, and mtime bypassing pathsec ENFORCE
findings.summary:
## Summary

`StreamBackedCorpusView`, a public API in `nltk/corpus/reader/util.py`, applies the pathsec sandbox to the file content it reads but not to the file metadata it probes in its constructor. When the view is created with a plain string fileid, `__init__` calls `os.stat(self._fileid).st_size` with no pathsec validation, so an application that passes an attacker influenced path to the constructor discloses whether an arbitrary out of root file exists and, if it does, its exact byte size and modification time, even when `nltk.pathsec.ENFORCE` is `True`. This is the residual metadata channel left open by the fix for CVE-2026-63312 (GHSA-x5ph-mj9p-rfr8), which closed arbitrary content read on the same code path but did not bring the sibling `os.stat` under the sandbox.

## Root Cause

The pathsec sandbox is intended to confine all NLTK filesystem access to allowed data roots. The fix for CVE-2026-63312 enforced this for content reads by routing `StreamBackedCorpusView._open` through `nltk.pathsec.open` (`_secure_open`). The constructor, however, computes the end of file position eagerly, and on the non `PathPointer` branch it stats the caller supplied path directly. The `PathPointer` branch is validated (it calls `PathPointer.file_size()`), but the plain string branch reaches `os.stat` with no `validate_path`, `_secure_open`, or `required_root` check. The security invariant "no filesystem access outside allowed roots under ENFORCE" is therefore violated for the metadata channel: `os.stat` is filesystem access, and it is performed on the same untrusted string entry point that the content read fix protected.

```text
Guarded sibling: _open() (routes through nltk.pathsec.open); the constructor os.stat is not guarded
```

findings.title: NLTK: Untrusted search path in prover9/mace4 config allows local code execution via relative binary_location
findings.summary:
## Summary
`Prover9Parent.config_prover9(binary_location=...)` (and `Mace`, which inherits it) accepts a relative `binary_location` and passes it as `path_to_bin` to `find_binary`, which disables the CWD-relative rejection guard. Unlike the boxer/senna/malt/repp siblings, prover9/mace apply no `os.path.isabs()` filter, so the resolved relative program path (e.g. `./prover9`) is executed from the current working directory via `subprocess.Popen`. A local attacker who can plant `./prover9` (or `./mace4`) in the resolved directory achieves local code execution.

## Root Cause
`nltk/inference/prover9.py:121-135` calls `find_binary(name, path_to_bin=binary_location, env_vars=["PROVER9"], ...)`. A truthy `path_to_bin` sets `searching_bare_name = not path_to_bin and ...` → False (`internals.py:935`), so the guard `if searching_bare_name and not os.path.isabs(path): continue` (`internals.py:940`) never runs. The result is stored in `self._prover9_bin`; on the next `prove()`, `_call` → `subprocess.Popen([binary]+args, ...)` (`prover9.py:207`) execs it. `Mace(Prover9Parent)` inherits `config_prover9` (`mace.py:229`). By contrast boxer's `_find_binary` (`sem/boxer.py:251-266`) iterates `find_binary_iter` and returns only the first `os.path.isabs()` result; repp/malt/senna similarly reject a relative explicit bin dir. prover9/mace have no such filter.

## Impact
Local arbitrary code execution: an attacker-planted `./prover9`/`./mace4` runs as the invoking user when the application is configured with a relative `binary_location` and the attacker can write to the resolved directory.
